q: In cargo metadata output, how do you tell a workspace-internal dependency from an external one?
options: Internal dependency entries carry a `path` field pointing inside the workspace; external ones do not
Internal dependencies are listed under `workspace-dependencies`; external ones under `dependencies`
Internal dependencies have `req = "workspace"`; external ones have a version
There is no way: cargo metadata flattens both kinds into one list
explanation: `workspace-dependencies` is a table in Cargo.toml manifests, not a field in metadata JSON.
Version requirements exist in both kinds; `req` values are semver strings everywhere.
`--no-deps` metadata keeps both kinds in `dependencies`, distinguished by the optional `path`.

q: Why does goose split its data model and Provider trait into `goose-provider-types`?
options: So extension/author crates can compile against the trait + data model without pulling in the whole engine
To make the build faster by parallelizing compilation of two identical copies
Because crates.io requires traits to live in a separate crate from implementations
To hide the provider architecture from the goose-cli binary
explanation: There is a single copy of the types; splitting does not duplicate work.
crates.io has no such rule; many workspaces keep traits and impls in one crate.
The CLI uses these types too — the split is about who can depend on what, not hiding.

q: Which dependency direction is legal in the goose workspace?
options: goose-providers -> goose-provider-types -> (external only); goose -> goose-providers
goose-provider-types -> goose, since goose has more helpers available
goose -> goose-cli, because the CLI exposes the agent loop API
Any direction, as long as the cycle has an even number of edges
explanation: That edge would drag the entire engine into the sink crate, defeating its purpose.
The dependency arrow is the reverse: goose-cli depends on goose's library API.
Rust rejects all cycles, odd or even, regardless of arc count.

q: `crates/goose/src/lib.rs:15` does `pub mod conversation { pub use goose_providers::conversation::*; }`. What does this achieve?
options: Goose keeps consuming the datamodel from goose-providers while presenting it under its own module path
It creates a second, independent copy of the conversation types inside goose
It makes the conversation module private to the goose crate
It enables tree-shaking of unused conversation types at link time
explanation: A re-export is an alias, not a copy — the type identity stays `goose_providers::conversation::...`.
`pub mod` publicly re-exports; nothing is hidden here.
Rust does not tree-shake at link time via re-exports; a type used once is compiled once.

q: What does the `rankdir=BT` line in your l01-graph.dot do?
options: It draws the graph bottom-to-top so dependency sinks (type crates) sit at the bottom
It sorts nodes by binary-size descending
It tells GraphViz that the graph package is from crates.io
It is required for cycles to render
explanation: GraphViz does not know about binary sizes; that is not a DOT attribute.
`rankdir` controls layout direction only; provenance is irrelevant to DOT.
Cyclic graphs fail in `dot` regardless of rankdir.

q: A PR adds `goose = { path = "../goose" }` to `goose-provider-types/Cargo.toml`. Which change statement is TRUE?
options: The entire workspace becomes unbuildable due to a cycle until the edge is removed
It compiles fine but slows CI down slightly
cargo automatically drops the edge because it is a type-only crate
It only breaks if both crates export a type with the same name
explanation: A cycle anywhere breaks the whole workspace graph; cargo does not degrade gracefully.
Cargo never removes declared dependencies — it errors on the cycle.
Name collisions produce different errors; the cycle error fires first.
